claim: The cardboard boxes stacked floor-to-ceiling in the photographs of the 91st-floor World Trade Center studio were the camouflage, not the cargo. Gelitin — four Austrian artists, Wolfgang Gantner, Florian Reither, Ali Janka and Tobias Urban — held a six-month lease on the space through the Lower Manhattan Cultural Council's residency program for artists, and built a wooden enclosure and a wall of boxes to screen the balcony they were secretly assembling, so that anyone who wandered in would take the boxes themselves for the artwork. In March 2000 they removed a window pane and the balcony stood outside the tower for about nineteen minutes. No source identifies what the boxes held; the reading of them as cartons of electrical fuse holders originates in social-media commentary, not in the collective's book, the residency records, or any reporting on the project. The group is Austrian and has no documented connection to the Israeli nationals described in the DEA's 2001 report.

sources.label: Spike Art Magazine, "One Work: Gelitin's 'The B-Thing'" — account of the studio, the wooden enclosure and the purpose of the boxes.
sources.quote: the idea was that someone familiar with the group could easily assume that the 'art' they were working on was the boxes, or in the boxes, or some sort of combination of the two

sources.label: Wikipedia, "Gelitin" — the six-month lease via the Lower Manhattan Cultural Council, the members, and the duration of the installation.
sources.quote: a six-month lease in a vacant space at the 91st floor of the World Trade Center's North Tower (WTC1), where the lease was secured through a Lower Manhattan Cultural Council program for resident artists

sources.label: Gelitin, "The B-Thing" (Boymans/Walther König, 2001) — the collective's own 55-page photographic record of the installation.
Rolling Stone, "The Artwork That Spawned 9/11 Conspiracy Theories and Mystery" — feature on the project and the claims attached to it.

notes: Written against a specific conflation: the Austrian collective Gelitin and the Israeli nationals in the DEA report are two separate stories that get fused into one. The fuse-holder identification ("BB-18", Littelfuse of Chicago) traces to social-media annotation of the book's photographs; searches return no documentation of the box contents from any source, including the artists, the council, or the reporting. Rolling Stone 402s our fetcher behind a paywall proxy, so the Spike and Wikipedia quotes carry the verbatim. The installation itself is recorded separately in 2000-gelitin-001; the DEA report in 2001-art-students-001.
